templates.title: Clinical risk management system (CRMS)
templates.purpose: A short practice document that says how you do clinical safety for every digital tool. Written once, used for all of them.
templates.who: Written by the CSO and practice manager. Approved by the partners.

rows: The partners, at the practice meeting on 12/01/2026

blocks.x: This document sets out how the practice manages clinical risk when it introduces, changes, uses and switches off digital tools (health IT systems), in line with the NHS standard DCB0160. It applies to every tool that could affect patient care, whoever bought it.

rows: Accountable for clinical safety in the practice. Accept the remaining risk before a tool goes live.
A registered clinician trained in clinical risk management. Leads the assessment and signs the safety case report.
Keeps the technology register and the safety documents. Organises workshops, training and reviews.
Use tools as trained, follow the controls, and report problems and near misses.

blocks.x: If your CSO is external or shared across your PCN, say so here and how to contact them.
For each tool, we follow five stages. The paperwork matches the risk: a minor change may need one line in the hazard log, a new clinical tool needs the full set.

Assess: hold a hazard workshop and write the hazard log.
Approve: the CSO writes and signs the safety case report; the partners accept the remaining risk.
Go live: train staff, put the controls in place, tell patients.
Monitor and review: record incidents, check the controls work, and review the hazard log.

templates.title: Hazard log
templates.purpose: Every hazard you’ve found for one tool, written as cause, effect, hazard and harm, with the controls and the risk before and after.
templates.who: The CSO owns it. The team adds to it at the workshop and after incidents.
templates.when: Started at the hazard workshop. Updated after incidents, changes and reviews.

cols.g: What could make it happen, usually the technology or how it’s used. Often more than one
What goes wrong with the information first
The situation where a person, usually the patient, could come to harm
What could happen to the patient
Why you chose this likelihood and severity: incidents, supplier data, local experience
Controls that stop the cause leading to the hazard; mitigations that limit harm if it happens. Include supplier controls

cols.n: Evidence the controls are in place
cols.g: How you know: setting checked, training record, audit, test
Why the controls bring the score down, and by how much

ex: The patient chooses an admin or "ask a question" route but includes red-flag symptoms. The form’s questions don’t pick up the red flag. The patient goes back and changes answers after a red-flag warning.
A request describing red-flag symptoms is triaged as routine
A patient with red-flag symptoms is not directed to an urgent assessment in time
Delayed treatment of a serious condition, such as sepsis, a heart attack or a suicidal crisis; at worst, death
Supplier’s DCB0129 hazard log rates under-triage as its top risk. In a one-week sample of 50 requests, 2 described possible red flags under an admin route.

Controls: A banner at the start of the form tells patients to call 999 or 111 for red-flag symptoms. Red-flag answers stop the form from going further and direct the patient to 999 or 111. The supplier confirms in writing that changing answers after a red-flag warning is logged and flagged. Requests sent as “ask the GP a question” go straight to the duty GP, so any symptoms in them are seen quickly. Mitigations: Every request that mentions symptoms is reviewed by the duty doctor within two hours in core hours. A safety-netting message about red-flag symptoms is shown when the form is sent.
Form screenshots and test cases on file. Duty doctor rota and audit spreadsheet.
Red-flag stop tested with 10 test cases before go-live, all stopped. Duty doctor review times audited monthly: 96% within two hours in the first month.
The tool books some requests straight into a routine slot, or sends the patient a booking link, using the patient’s answers to set questions. Nobody reads the free text before the appointment.
Important detail written in the free text, such as weight loss or a new lump, sits unread until the routine appointment
A patient whose problem needs an earlier or different assessment waits for a routine appointment
Delayed diagnosis, for example of cancer, and delayed treatment
Audit of 30 auto-booked requests found 3 with free text a GP judged should have been seen sooner.

Controls: Only admin and clearly routine request types are set to auto-book; anything with symptoms goes to a person first. Free text containing set words (for example lump, bleeding, weight loss) is sent to the duty doctor instead of being auto-booked. Mitigations: A care navigator reads the free text of every auto-booked request the same working day and escalates anything worrying.
Auto-book settings export and keyword list on file. Same-day read recorded in the care navigation log.
Repeat audit after the change: 0 of 30. Auto-book settings exported from the tool and checked by the CSO.
The form stays open in the evening and at weekends with nobody watching it. On busy days or during leave, nobody owns the queue. A request is assigned to a clinician who has gone home.
A request sits unread for hours or days
A patient’s request is not actioned when it needs to be, while they believe the practice is dealing with it
Delayed assessment and treatment; the problem may get worse
Before the change, 15% of requests arrived outside core hours, and 4 in one month waited more than a working day.

Controls: Symptom requests can only be sent in core hours; outside them, the form directs patients to 111 or 999. A named owner for the queue every session, on the rota. Mitigations: An end-of-day check that the queue is empty or handed over. The first job on a Monday is any request that arrived at the weekend.
Supplier settings screenshot. Queue owner rota. End-of-day check log.
Form hours confirmed in the supplier settings. End-of-day checks signed off on the care navigation log, audited monthly.
A parent or carer submits for someone else using their own details, or the patient’s details don’t match the record
The request is attached to the wrong patient’s record
The right patient isn’t assessed, and decisions are made using the wrong patient’s record
Missed or delayed care for the patient who needed it; the wrong treatment or advice for the other
Supplier’s hazard log lists patient-matching errors. Two near misses in the first month, both requests from parents.

Controls: The form asks who the request is for and collects the patient’s own details. Staff check name, date of birth and NHS number before filing. Mitigations: Requests made on someone else’s behalf are flagged for a second check before a clinician acts on them.
Care navigation protocol v2. Training record. Incident log.
Filing check added to the care navigation protocol; all care navigators trained. No further near misses in three months.
As more same-day appointments are released through the online form, fewer are left for patients who phone or walk in
Patients who can’t use the form find no appointments left
A patient who can’t use the form, because of age, disability, language or no internet, is assessed later than they need to be
Delayed care for patients already more likely to come to harm
In the first fortnight, all same-day appointments had gone by 9:30 on four days, mostly to online requests.

Controls: A fixed share of same-day appointments is kept for phone and walk-in requests. Reception can fill in the form on a patient’s behalf. Mitigations: Access data and complaints by route reviewed at the quarterly clinical governance meeting.
Appointment template shows the reserved slots. Quarterly review minuted at clinical governance.

It applies to everyone who works here, including locums, trainees, students and contractors. It covers any AI tool used for practice work: tools we buy, tools the ICB or NHS England provides, AI features added to software we already use, and apps on personal devices.

blocks.label: How patients are told, and how they can say no
blocks.ex: Our privacy notice, website and waiting room posters explain which AI tools we use and why. For Wren Scribe, the clinician tells the patient at the start, respects a no, and records the answer. Patients can always contact us by phone or in person: AI is never the only way to get care here.

blocks.label: How you check the tools, and how often
blocks.ex: For the first three months of a new tool, the CSO checks a sample of its output each month. After that, each tool is audited at least once a year. We check whether tools work equally well for all our patients, including people with strong accents, disabilities or limited English.

blocks.label: How problems are reported and learned from
blocks.ex: Report any problem or near miss through our incident process the same day. The CSO reviews it and decides whether to pause the tool. If patient information went somewhere it shouldn’t, tell the DPO straight away: it’s a data breach. We report to the supplier and, where relevant, Learn from Patient Safety Events and the MHRA Yellow Card scheme. Incidents and what we learned are discussed at our monthly clinical governance meeting.

blocks.label: Training and induction
blocks.ex: Staff are trained on each tool before they use it, and training is recorded. New staff, locums and trainees are shown this policy and the register at induction.

blocks.x: This policy and the register are reviewed every year alongside the DSPT, or sooner if a tool, national guidance or the law changes.
